title: Ancient DNA Links Ice Age Europeans Across the Continent
paragraphs: A study published in Science Advances has used ancient DNA to reassess how Europeans were connected during the Ice Age. Led by the University of Vienna, with 37 authors, it centres on the Gravettian culture, which spread across Europe from roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.

The key evidence is the genome of a woman who lived about 30,000 years ago in Isturitz Cave, in France, the oldest genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Although most of her ancestry was western, she also carried central and eastern European ancestry, and modelling dates the mixing to about 32,500–31,500 years ago. “Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” said first author Pere Gelabert.

The researchers also extracted DNA from sediment in a 22,000-year-old layer at El Mirón Cave, in northern Spain, where no human bones or teeth survive. They argue that this supports the Iberian Peninsula as a refuge during the coldest phase of the Ice Age. Several limitations apply: the central finding rests on a single individual, the press release does not mention funding, and some of the interpretations are described as only likely. The picture is promising, but still preliminary.

questions.q: What does the Isturitz genome suggest?
questions.a: That eastern and western European populations mixed.

questions.q: How did the team get DNA without human bones?
questions.a: From sediment in a cave layer.

questions.q: What is one limitation of the study?
questions.a: The main finding rests on a single individual.
